newsitem.title: USA: Trucking group plans lawsuit against EPA air plan.
newsitem.headline: Trucking group plans lawsuit against EPA air plan.

text.p: A trucking group Friday said it planned to file a lawsuit challenging an Environmental Protection Agency plan to tighten curbs on smog and soot.

The EPA is set to issue the new clean air standards, which President Clinton endorsed this week, before a July 19 court-ordered deadline. Several business and industry groups fought to stop the EPA from setting the new standards and asked Congress to block the rules, but the trucking group was the first to announce that it would file a lawsuit.

"As soon as it's published in the Federal Register we will file the suit," Jim Lewis, spokesman for the American Trucking Associations, the largest U.S. group representing trucking companies, truck manufacturers and related businesses, said.

The group's president, Thomas Donohue, said it would argue that the EPA had "failed to live up to legal provisions of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act, which requires the agency to consider how the standards will impact small business." He said in a statement that the rules were based on "inadequate science."

The EPA said the new standards could be met largely by imposing controls on coal-fired power plants, but the trucking group said manufacturers would be forced to spend billions of dollars to develop a new generation of clean-burning engines.

Other groups have not yet decided whether to sue the EPA, but a spokesman for the American Petroleum Institute, an oil industry trade group, said there were questions about the legality of the agency's plan to give some areas more time than others to meet the new standards.

Under the Clean Air Act, all areas that do not meet air quality standards are supposed to be designated as out of compliance. But in a bid to ease concerns of cities that the new rules would cost industry billions of dollars and stifle investment in urban areas, the EPA said it would stretch the timetable for complying with the new standards in 33 Eastern states that already were planning steps to curb smog.
